newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Britain sees no quick end to EU beef ban.
newsitem.headline: Britain sees no quick end to EU beef ban.

text.p: Jack Cunningham, Britain's new Agriculture Minister, sought on Monday to make a quick start to improving relations with the European Union but did not see any early lifting of a world ban on British beef exports.

Only 10 days after Labour won a landslide victory in British elections, Cunningham met EU farm chief Franz Fischler to discuss prospects for lifting the 14-month-old ban, EU farm reform and plans for Britain's EU presidency in January 1998.
"We believe that a more constructive, open dialogue is going to be helpful," Cunningham told a news briefing after the talks.

But he declined to give any forecast for an end to the crippling ban, imposed in March 1996 after the former Conservative government admitted that mad cow disease, or bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), could be caught by humans.

"I think we can do better. I'm not setting any dates or putting any deadlines," he said, avoiding raising hopes that the EU would approve a British "certified herd scheme" to identify cows from BSE-free herds which could then be exported.
Cunningham said the former government's intransigeant and aggressive attitude was counter-productive.
"It beggars belief...that anyone could have really believed that it was possible to get the beef ban raised by November last year," he said, referring to former Prime Minister John Major's forecast.
Cunningham stressed Britain must adopt a balanced approach.
"We need to get the science right and also the politics," he said. "I don't believe that the phoney and counter-productive beef war did anything other than delay possible solutions."
Conservative tactics of blocking EU business to get the ban eased ahead of an EU summit in Florence in June 1996 helped harden continental attitudes against Britain.
Fischler told Cunningham that the lifting of the EU export ban on British beef was in the hands of various scientific committees, a European Commission agriculture spokesman said.
"We have repeated that we are bound by scientific advice," spokesman Gerard Kiely said, adding, "Mr Fischler looks forward to working with Minister Cunningham.
Cunningham welcomed Fischler's plans to make a fresh bid to ban cattle and sheep parts - brains, eyes, spinal cord -- most likely to transmit the disease from human and animal food.
"We don't want to import beef less stringently produced than our domestic beef," he said.
Although pledging a fresh start, Cunningham did not float any new ideas to end the beef ban or reform costly EU farm policies.
But he said the aim was to make progress on the beef ban and on cereals, beef and dairy reforms during Britain's six-month tenure of the EU presidency starting in January 1998.
